newsitem.title: USA: U.S. science, math education unfocused - study.
newsitem.headline: U.S. science, math education unfocused - study.

text.p: U.S. mathematics and science education lacks focus and the curriculum is "a mile wide and an inch deep" compared with those of other nations, according to a major study released on Tuesday.
The study, funded by the U.S. Department of Education, the National Science Foundation (NSF) and the Canadian government, did not include student achievement statistics or country rankings.

Instead the Third International Mathematics and Science Study looked at the content of curriculum and the style of teaching, and concluded that the U.S. math and science curricula were "aimed at the lowest common denominator."
"There is no single intellectual vision (in U.S. schools)," said William Schmidt, a Michigan State University education professor who coordinated the research. It included data from 49 countries.

"The findings do indicate that because U.S. science and math teachers are expected to teach a wide range of subjects, they seldom have the time to teach any in depth," said Dr. Neil Lane, NSF director.
The study noted that the United States did not have a single national curriculum, or common standards because authority is distributed among federal, state and local governments.
"There is no one at the helm...In truth, there is no helm," Schmidt told a Washington news conference.

"It is wishful optimism to expect our students to do well in science and, especially, in mathematics compared to students in other countries in light of our fragmented curriculum," the study concluded.
The study found that the content of school mathematics and science is not universal.

"Content varies considerably across countries, not only in terms of the mathematics and science topics studied in school but also in the degree and type of focus they recieve, and in the types of skills that students are expected to acquire," the report concluded.
